title: Continuous Diffusion Models Can Obey Formal Syntax
claim: A discrete syntactic constraint can be scored analytically by multiplying automaton transition matrices with per-position token probabilities from the latent.
layout: 4 regions, automaton top-left, matrices right, worked equation bottom-right, color-coded entries
description: The figure is a worked toy example. At top left is a finite automaton for the regex c(a|u)t. It has states q0 to q4, with q4 double-circled as accepting. Edges are labeled c, a, u and t, and the a, u and t labels are colored red, green and orange. Below it is a 5x3 matrix x_t. Rows are the vocabulary a, c, r, t, u, and columns are positions c1 to c3. It holds the per-position token probabilities from the latent. On the right are three 5x5 transition matrices M1, M2 and M3, with rows and columns indexed by q0 to q4. Their nonzero entries share colors with the matching automaton edges and probabilities. At bottom right, an equation multiplies the start vector by M1·M2·M3 and evaluates to 0.28. The eye goes first to the colorful matrices.
caption: The automaton for the regex c(a|u)t describing the regular constraint L = {cat, cut}, the unigram distribution Dec(xt) defined by the current latent xt on a vocabulary {a, c, r, t, u} of size 5, and transition matrices for this automaton and latent space for a sequence of length 3. Valid transitions inside the automaton and their probabilities are color-coded.
abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their global, non-causal generation process, but their continuous latent dynamics make discrete constraints -- e.g., the output should be a JSON file that matches a given schema -- difficult to impose. We introduce a training-free guidance method for steering continuous diffusion language models to satisfy formal syntactic constraints expressed using regular expressions. Our approach constructs an analytic score estimating the probability that a latent state decodes to a valid string accepted by a given regular expression, and uses its gradient to guide sampling, without training auxiliary classifiers. The denoising process targets the base model conditioned on syntactic validity. We implement our method in Diffinity on top of the PLAID diffusion model and evaluate it on 180 regular-expression constraints over JSON and natural-language benchmarks. Diffinity achieves 68-96\% constraint satisfaction while incurring only a small perplexity cost relative to unconstrained sampling, outperforming autoregressive constrained decoding in both constraint satisfaction and output quality. Diffinity is open-sourced at github.com/large-loris-models/Diffinity.
